newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- US jobs seen confirming Fed-on-hold view.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- US jobs seen confirming Fed-on-hold view.

text.p: The U.S. probably created a below-average number of jobs last month, adding to the batch of evidence that the Federal Reserve acted prudently last week when it held short-term interest rates steady, experts said.

"For this month's payrolls number, it's going to confirm that the Fed did the right thing last Tuesday when it elected to do nothing (to monetary policy)," said Christopher Rupkey, vice president and an economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
The government will report September nonfarm payrolls and monthly jobless rate on Friday, October 4, at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Economists in a Reuters survey predicted, on average, that 166,000 new jobs were added to U.S. payrolls last month.
That compares to 250,000 in August, and more than 200,000 each month since May.

The unemployment rate, meanwhile, is forecast to have risen a notch to 5.2 percent. August's reading of 5.1 percent marked the lowest jobless rate since March of 1989 when it stood at 5.0 percent, according to the Labor Department.
A drop in the number of local government hirings -- primarily teachers -- and a cooling in manufacturing probably held back jobs growth in September, pundits postulated.
Government payrolls grew by 77,000 in August, and manufacturing created 25,000 new jobs. Manufacturing had lost a total of 32,000 jobs in June and July combined.
Rupkey of Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi said factories probably added no more than 5,000 new positions in September, and he downplayed that sector's burst of growth in August.
"The growth in manufacturing was only a one-month rise," he said. "We may see a very small rise this month -- maybe 5,000 -- showing manufacturing really isn't recovering."
Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi forecast 125,000 new jobs were created last month and pegged the jobless rate at 5.3 percent.

The jobs data will confirm the view that the Fed acted wisely last month when it opted to keep short-term interest rates steady. The central bank's policymaking arm concluded its September 24 confab with no change to rates.
The overnight bank lending, or federal funds rate, remains at 5.25 percent, unchanged since January 31 when the Fed cut rates by 0.25 percentage point. The discount rate is firm at 5.0 percent.
Adding to the Fed-on-hold view is the fact policymakers will have another jobs report -- data for October -- which will be released before the next policy gathering on November 13.
Experts said those figures could tell a different story.
"We'll see (payrolls) above 200,000 for the balance of the year, and a jobless rate possibly at 5.0 percent and maybe below," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
If his projections materialize, Moran said the economy probably won't be able to tolerate such a low unemployment rate and still keep inflation in check.
"I think we're seeing some early warning signs that wages are beginning to show (signs of inflation)," he said. "The Fed will not be able to sit by idly."
Rupkey of Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi agreed. In keeping with the data's "sawtooth pattern" of recent months, he said his preliminary forecast calls for October payrolls to swell in excess of 300,000.

"Payrolls are up one month, down below trend the next and then right back up again," Rupkey said. "October payrolls will be really important. That will be right in front of when Fed policymakers take their vote ... These (September payrolls) are pretty much dead on arrival."
Average hourly earnings, the employment report's wage gauge, are expected to rise 0.2 percent in September, and the workweek probably lengthened to 34.5 hours, according to the Reuters survey.
In August, earnings rose 0.5 percent and the workweek ran 34.4 hours.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1661
